title: The Irish Elk

paragraphs.text: The giant deer, or Irish elk, must have cut a magnificent figure, standing more than two metres at the shoulder and carrying a spread of antlers 3.5 metres across. This spectacular beast was thought to have become extinct at the end of the Pleistocene era around 10,500 years ago, during the cooling of the climate known as the Last Ice Age. But results of a recent study led by Professor Tony Stuart of University College London indicate that Irish elk in fact survived several millennia longer in western Siberia. His evidence points to the persistence of the species in the southern Ural mountains on the Europe-Asia border as late as only 7,500 years ago, and therefore into the age of modern man.

Using radiocarbon dating of Irish elk specimens from various locations, Stuart's team have shown that the species was widespread throughout Europe and Asia (Eurasia) more than 20,000 years ago. But by the end of the Last Glacial Maximum, the prolonged cold spell occurring around 15,000 years ago, they had disappeared from everywhere but the plains of central Asia. From there, Irish elk apparently recolonised north-western Europe during the subsequent period of climatic warming. They made a last stand in the British Isles before finally dying out there 10,500 years ago, while the Siberian population apparently persisted for a further 3,000 years.

Theories about the disappearance of the Irish elk often focus on its huge antlers which posed a large annual nutritional burden on the male deer, and would also be physically unwieldy in dense forests. So both physical and nutritional constraints probably restricted the Irish elk to those fertile open environments which supported the growth of moderate-stature willow and birch shrubs. This type of vegetation could be navigated, while still providing sufficient calcium and phosphate, important for antler growth. These ideal conditions were widespread in the British Isles until the Last Ice Age, when the landscape rapidly became treeless tundra, frozen hard in winter and supporting mainly damp, ground-hugging mosses in summer.

In Siberia, however, it appears that the necessary temperate and nutrient-rich grass/shrub plant community persisted for much longer. It seems that a general spread of dry grassy plains (steppes) over western Siberia, and the persistence of closed forests in the mountains, eventually squeezed the Irish elk's habitat to a narrow sliver, and contributed to the extinction of the last population. In contrast, woolly mammoths, who apparently thrived on steppe grassland, lived on well beyond the extinction of the Irish elk. There is evidence of this species persisting on Wrangel Island in north-eastern Siberia a mere 4,000 years ago. Stuart et al effectively link the shifts in Irish elk and woolly mammoth populations, to data from fossilised plants showing climate-driven changes in the vegetation which sustained them.

In recent years, ecologists have shown that large plant-eating animals not only respond to changes in the composition of plant communities, but also themselves control this composition, through selective feeding on preferred plant species. Intriguingly, by trampling over tundra mosses and stimulating grass growth through grazing, the woolly mammoth might have helped to maintain and expand its own preferred dry steppe habitat, even when the climate was cool enough to support mossy tundra. The shift to tundra in Siberia might have happened only after human hunters had eradicated woolly mammoths, thus relieving both trampling pressure on mosses and competition with grasses that were previously stimulated by grazing.

The Irish elk may well have strengthened its hold on its Siberian habitat in the same way. Why then, once it had survived the changes wrought by the Last Ice Age, did the remaining population not recover and expand again, as it had done in previous millennia? One obvious answer lies in human development: by 7,500 years ago prehistoric man had settled into substantial communities of hunter-gatherers, a situation which must surely have had a significant impact on Irish elk populations.

The roles played by humans and climate in Ice Age extinctions vary considerably from one continent to another. The continent of Africa lost almost no large species, despite climate change and the presence of humans for millions of years. Australia, by contrast, underwent little or no climate change, yet lost 21 genera of large mammals within thirty millennia of the arrival of modern man. Meanwhile in Eurasia, two vast waves of extinctions coincided with drops in temperature - a prolonged Ice Age between 45,000 and 20,000 years ago, and the final cold snap that began about 12,000 years ago and lasted for two millennia. This second climate change was enough to almost-but not completely-eradicate the Irish elk. For Stuart and his team, the discovery that the population was able to survive in isolated pockets into the era of modern man considerably weakens the argument that climate change was wholly responsible for the ultimate demise of the species. The evidence of his team's investigations suggests that whereas climatic warming and cooling indeed set the stage through broad-scale vegetation changes, it was the human hunter who may well have delivered the fatal blow.
